documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
49M establishing care. No PCP since moving to the US in 2019; before that, care was sporadic and he has no records to send. Works construction (laborer, mostly framing and demo).

Alcohol: up front about it. Drinks about 6 beers a day, has for roughly 20 years. Has been through withdrawal before, several times, treated in EDs; can't give dates. Longest dry spells 1 to 3 months, then back to it. Not interested in a program today but willing to keep talking.
Tobacco: smokes, about a pack a day on and off since his late 20s. Thinking about quitting.
No drugs.

PMH: nothing he knows of. PSH: none. Meds: none. NKDA.
FH: father had alcohol use disorder and died with cirrhosis. Mother type 2 diabetes. Brother has high blood pressure; he lives with his brother and his brother's family.

ROS: appetite fair, no abdominal pain, no jaundice he's noticed, no GI bleeding. No chest pain or dyspnea.

Exam: thin man, NAD. Anicteric. Heart RRR, lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, liver edge not palpable, no ascites. No spider angiomata. No tremor today. Gait normal.

AUDIT-C 10. PHQ-9 5.

A/P
1. Severe alcohol use disorder. Long talk. Not ready to cut back much; agreed to come back in a few months. Gave him the outpatient addiction services list. Start thiamine 100 daily, folic acid 1 mg daily, multivitamin.
2. Liver: check CMP, CBC, GGT; hep C and hep B serologies; RUQ ultrasound.
3. Tobacco: advised quitting, he'll think about it.
4. Health maintenance: flu shot next month with RN. Colorectal screening due, FIT at that visit.

documents.title: Your blood work
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Rohan, your liver tests are up: AST 68, ALT 47 and GGT 290. That pattern fits alcohol affecting the liver. Liver function itself (bilirubin, albumin) is OK, and your blood counts are fine. Hepatitis C test is negative. Your hepatitis B tests show you have never had it and are not immune, so I'd like to vaccinate you; we can start that at a follow-up. The ultrasound is scheduled for 9/28.

reports.text:
Indication: elevated transaminases, heavy alcohol use.
Technique: grayscale and color Doppler sonography of the right upper quadrant.
Liver: normal in size. Diffusely increased echogenicity with mild attenuation of the sound beam. No focal lesion. Hepatic contour smooth.
Gallbladder: normal wall, no stones, no pericholecystic fluid. Sonographic Murphy sign negative.
Bile ducts: no intrahepatic ductal dilatation. Common duct 4 mm.
Portal vein: patent with normal hepatopetal flow.
Pancreas: head and body unremarkable where seen; tail obscured by bowel gas.
Right kidney: normal size, no hydronephrosis.
Spleen: normal in size.
No ascites.
reports.conclusion: Diffusely echogenic liver consistent with hepatic steatosis. No focal liver lesion. No biliary dilatation.

documents.title: Result note
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Steatosis on US, nothing focal, spleen normal size. With the enzyme pattern and his intake this is alcoholic liver disease. Added to problem list. RN to call.

CC: weight loss, loose stools.

HPI: About six months now of loose stools that he describes as big, greasy and smelling terrible, hard to flush. Several a day. Over the same stretch he has lost weight without trying; down to 55 kg from 61 at his first visit here. Also gets episodes of pain high in the belly that bores through to his back, worse after a big meal. No vomiting, no black or bloody stools, no fevers.
Alcohol: stopped drinking at the start of December after a bad weekend, about ten days dry so far. No shakes this time.
FIT kit from October not returned.

Exam: thin, temporal wasting. Anicteric today. Abdomen soft, tender in the epigastrium, no rebound, no guarding, no mass. No edema.

A/P
1. Weight loss with steatorrhea and epigastric pain radiating to the back in a long-term heavy drinker: concerning for chronic pancreatitis with malabsorption. Referring to GI, asked for the soonest slot. CMP and CBC today.
2. AUD: newly abstinent. Encouraged; reviewed withdrawal warning signs and to go to the ED for confusion, shaking or seizures if he drinks and stops again.
3. Continue thiamine, folate, MVI.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GASTROENTEROLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of service: 01/05/2023
Referred by: primary care

Reason for referral: weight loss and chronic diarrhea.

Mr. Chowdhury is a 50-year-old construction laborer with a long history of heavy alcohol use and known alcoholic liver disease. For roughly half a year he has had bulky, oily, malodorous stools along with recurrent epigastric pain that bands through to the back. He has lost weight steadily. He has been abstinent for about a month.

Current medications: thiamine 100 mg daily, folic acid 1 mg daily, multivitamin daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: father with alcohol use disorder and cirrhosis; mother with type 2 diabetes; brother with hypertension.
Social: former smoker, about 20 pack-years, quit 2022. Heavy beer use for two decades, currently abstinent.

Exam: cachectic. Mild scleral icterus. Abdomen with epigastric tenderness, no rebound or guarding. Bowel sounds normal. No ascites.

Data: amylase 160 U/L (30-110), lipase 300 U/L (0-160), fecal elastase <100 mcg/g (>200), total cholesterol 145, triglycerides 88.

Impression:
1. Chronic pancreatitis, alcohol related, with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency; markedly low fecal elastase with classic steatorrhea.
2. Protein-calorie malnutrition.
3. Alcohol use disorder, currently abstinent.

Recommendations:
- Pancrelipase 36,000 lipase units with each meal and 18,000 units with snacks; prescription sent. Take at the start of the meal.
- Continue thiamine, folate and multivitamin.
- Strict abstinence from alcohol.
- Return to GI as needed; primary care to follow weight.

Thank you for this referral.

documents.title: Neurology Consultation
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
OUTPATIENT NEUROLOGY CONSULTATION
Visit date: 07/06/2023

Reason: gait instability.

History: 51-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder and chronic pancreatitis on enzyme replacement, referred for half a year of steadily worsening walking and balance. He now needs to hold onto furniture moving about his house. He denies limb weakness, numbness or pain. He reports about two months of abstinence.

Medications: pancrelipase with meals and snacks, thiamine 100 mg, folic acid 1 mg, multivitamin.
Allergies: none known.
Social: construction laborer. Former smoker, 20 pack-years. Long history of daily beer, 6 a day for about 20 years, with repeated withdrawal episodes and abstinent periods of 1 to 3 months.
Family: father alcohol use disorder with cirrhosis, mother type 2 diabetes, brother hypertension.

Examination: alert, fluent, speech without dysarthria. Extraocular movements full, no nystagmus. Strength 5/5 throughout. Sensation intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration and proprioception. Reflexes 2+ and symmetric, toes downgoing. Finger-to-nose accurate even with eyes closed. Gait wide-based and unsteady; unable to tandem walk.

Laboratory (drawn at this visit): CBC normal. AST and ALT mildly elevated. Vitamin B12 normal. TSH normal. Serum thiamine low.

Impression: midline (truncal) cerebellar syndrome with gait ataxia and preserved limb coordination, in the setting of chronic alcohol use and low thiamine: alcoholic cerebellar degeneration. Thiamine deficiency.

Recommendations: abstinence is the key intervention. Thiamine 100 mg daily, taken every day. Return in about six months.

Thank you for the opportunity to see him.

Active: severe AUD (abstinent since May 2023), alcoholic liver disease, chronic pancreatitis with EPI on pancrelipase, protein-calorie malnutrition, alcoholic cerebellar degeneration, thiamine deficiency. Former smoker, 20 pk-yr, quit Jan 2022.
Meds: pancrelipase 36,000 units with meals and 18,000 with snacks; thiamine 100 daily; folic acid 1 mg daily; MVI. NKDA.

He feels well. Five months dry, by far his best stretch. Gait the same. No falls. Eating three meals.

Exam: thin, anicteric, no stigmata of chronic liver disease. HEENT unremarkable. Heart RRR without murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender today. No edema. Neuro: wide-based gait, mild truncal sway, strength normal. Skin without rash.

PHQ-9 4.

Prevention: flu, updated COVID and Shingrix #1 today; Shingrix #2 in 2 to 6 months. FIT kit given (last one negative 2021; 2022 kit never came back). Lung cancer screening: eligible by age and pack-years, explained low-dose CT; he would rather wait, "enough tests this year." Will revisit. Hep B series complete. Tdap 2021. PCV20 2022. Labs today incl lipids.

NEUROLOGY FOLLOW-UP
Visit date: 01/15/2024

Seen in follow-up six months after his first visit for gait ataxia attributed to alcoholic cerebellar degeneration. He describes continued decline over the interval, now with frequent falls. No head strike and no loss of consciousness. His brother, who accompanies him, has noticed he is more forgetful and has more trouble with tasks that need coordinated hand use.

Medications: pancrelipase, thiamine 100 mg daily, folic acid, multivitamin. NKDA.

Exam: gait wide-based and unsteady. Rapid alternating movements impaired bilaterally. Intention tremor on reaching. Tone reduced in all four limbs. Reflexes normal. Sensation intact.

Labs today: AST 72 U/L, ALT 55 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 130 U/L, GGT 450 U/L.

Assessment: progression of alcoholic cerebellar degeneration, now with appendicular signs. The liver enzymes suggest ongoing alcohol exposure.

Plan: complete abstinence strongly advised; continue thiamine daily. Return in 6 months.

documents.title: Infectious Disease Consultation
documents.author: infectious disease
documents.body:
INFECTIOUS DISEASE CONSULTATION
Date: 09/08/2024
Reason: thoracic vertebral destruction, evaluate for infection.

52-year-old construction worker with severe alcohol use disorder, chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency and alcoholic cerebellar degeneration, admitted with mid-back pain. The pain is deep and constant, worse at night, and not touched by over-the-counter analgesics. Two months of night sweats and fatigue, with about 6 kg of unintended weight loss. He has not been in to see a doctor for some months. No known HIV. He came to the US in 2019 and works in construction.

Meds: pancrelipase, thiamine, folic acid, multivitamin. NKDA.

Vitals: T 37.8 C (100.0 F), BP 124/70, HR 88, RR 16.
Exam: moderate point tenderness over T9-T10. No visible deformity or gibbus. Neurologic exam normal: strength, sensation and reflexes intact in the legs, no sensory level.

Data: WBC 7,800/uL, hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, ESR 96 mm/hr, CRP 8.1 mg/dL.
Chest x-ray: apical scarring.
MRI thoracic spine: destruction of the anterior vertebral bodies of T9 and T10 with collapse of the intervening disc and a prevertebral fluid collection.

Impression: subacute thoracic spondylodiscitis with paraspinal collection and constitutional symptoms; tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) is the leading diagnosis given apical scarring and the anterior-body pattern.

Recommendations: CT-guided aspiration of the prevertebral collection for AFB smear, TB NAAT and mycobacterial culture plus routine cultures. HIV testing. Airborne isolation per protocol. Hold antimicrobials until sampled.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 09/07/2024, discharged 09/16/2024.

Principal diagnosis: tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease), T9-T10, with prevertebral collection.
Secondary: anemia of chronic disease; severe alcohol use disorder; chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency; alcoholic cerebellar degeneration; alcoholic liver disease; protein-calorie malnutrition.

Course: admitted from the ED with back pain and constitutional symptoms. MRI as described by ID. CT-guided aspiration of the prevertebral collection on 9/10: AFB smear positive; TB NAAT positive, rifampin resistance not detected. Culture pending. HIV antigen/antibody nonreactive. Started isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol with pyridoxine on 9/11, weight-based for 52 kg. Neurologically intact throughout; nonoperative management. No alcohol withdrawal during the stay. Hemoglobin 10.6 with normal MCV, attributed to chronic inflammation.

Discharge medications: isoniazid 300 mg daily, rifampin 600 mg daily, pyrazinamide 1000 mg daily, ethambutol 800 mg daily, pyridoxine 50 mg daily (TB drugs by DOT through the health department TB clinic); pancrelipase as before; thiamine 100 mg daily; folic acid 1 mg daily; multivitamin daily. Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: TB clinic, directly observed therapy starting 9/17; primary care within 1 to 2 weeks; monthly liver tests through TB clinic. Avoid alcohol entirely while on TB treatment.

documents.title: Post-hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hospital follow-up, discharged 9/16. Summary reviewed.

TB of the spine (T9-T10) confirmed by aspirate; on RIPE + B6 by DOT. TB clinic nurse comes to the house every morning; he likes her. Orange urine expected, he was told. Back pain 5/10, better than before admission. Night sweats easing. No leg weakness, no bowel or bladder trouble. Not drinking since admission; says it's easier with someone at the door every day.
Weight 52.

Exam: afebrile. Tender over lower thoracic spine. Strength 5/5 in legs, sensation intact. Gait wide-based as before.

A/P
- Pott disease: TB clinic directs treatment. Med list updated. LFTs today too since he has alcoholic liver disease and is on INH/RIF/PZA; TB clinic will also check monthly.
- Anemia of chronic disease: recheck in 2 to 3 months.
- AUD: abstinent 2.5 weeks. Encouraged. 
- Malnutrition: weight down 6 kg; enzymes with every meal.
We missed him in May; he says he "just didn't come." No judgment, glad he's here. RTC December.

documents.title: TB Clinic Progress Letter
documents.author: TB clinic
documents.body:
TB CLINIC, PROGRESS LETTER
Visit 10/22/2024

Your patient continues directly observed therapy for tuberculous spondylitis. The aspirate culture from 9/10 has finalized: tuberculosis complex, susceptible to isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. He has taken every observed dose so far. Monthly liver tests have been acceptable for his baseline. Vision screening unchanged on ethambutol. Back pain improving.

Plan: continue four drugs through the 2-month intensive phase, then isoniazid and rifampin. Household contacts have been evaluated by our program.

TB CLINIC, TREATMENT COMPLETION
Visit 03/11/2025

Your patient has completed 6 months of directly observed therapy for drug-susceptible tuberculous spondylitis of T9-T10: isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months, with pyridoxine. All medications stopped today.

MRI thoracic spine 03/04/2025: interval healing at T9-T10; the prevertebral collection has resolved; no new bone destruction.

He is asymptomatic apart from mild residual stiffness. He is discharged from TB clinic. Please contact us for any recurrent back pain, fever or night sweats.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Finished TB treatment 3/11, completion letter and MRI (healing, collection gone) reviewed. Back just a little stiff in the mornings. No sweats, weight 56.
Hgb 12.9 and ESR 18 today: anemia has resolved and inflammation is down. Pott disease and anemia of chronic disease marked resolved.
Alcohol: now that the DOT nurse isn't coming he's drinking again, most evenings. AUDIT-C 8. We talked about the pattern: he does well with daily structure. Offered the outpatient program and a daily check-in option again; declines for now but took the number.
EPI stable on enzymes. Cerebellar gait unchanged.
RTC 3 months, sooner for yellow eyes, belly pain or confusion.

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD
Arrival 05/10/2025 14:20

CC: belly pain and yellow eyes.

53-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency and alcoholic cerebellar degeneration, here with two weeks of worsening abdominal pain, jaundice and a falling appetite. Drinking about six beers daily, a pattern of roughly 20 years.

Meds: pancrelipase, thiamine, folic acid, multivitamin. NKDA.

T 38.3 C (100.9 F). Icteric sclerae. Liver enlarged and tender. Abdomen otherwise soft.

WBC 12.0, Hgb 13.2, platelets 95. AST 180, ALT 60, total bilirubin 6.2, direct 4.1, alkaline phosphatase 120. INR 1.6.

Impression: alcoholic hepatitis. Admit to medicine.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 05/10/2025, discharged 05/15/2025.

Diagnosis: alcoholic hepatitis.
Other: severe alcohol use disorder, alcoholic liver disease, chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency, alcoholic cerebellar degeneration, protein-calorie malnutrition, thiamine deficiency; history of tuberculous spondylitis, treated.

Course: fever on arrival prompted an infection workup: blood cultures no growth, urinalysis negative, chest x-ray clear. RUQ ultrasound showed an enlarged echogenic liver without biliary obstruction or ascites, portal vein patent. Managed with abstinence, nutrition support with enzyme replacement, IV then oral thiamine and withdrawal monitoring; no withdrawal symptoms developed. Fever resolved. Jaundice improving: bilirubin 4.8 and INR 1.4 on the day of discharge.

Discharge medications: unchanged home medications (pancrelipase with meals and snacks, thiamine 100 mg, folic acid 1 mg, multivitamin). NKDA.

Follow-up: primary care within one week with hepatic panel and INR. No alcohol.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen with brother after admission 5/10-5/15 for alcoholic hepatitis. Summary reviewed.

No alcohol since 5/9. Appetite slowly coming back. Belly much less sore. Eyes still yellow but less. No confusion, no black stool, no swelling.

Exam: afebrile. Scleral icterus. Liver edge palpable and mildly tender. No ascites, no asterixis.

Labs today: bilirubin 3.9 (4.8 at discharge), INR 1.3.

A/P
1. Alcoholic hepatitis, improving. Absolute abstinence. Weekly-ish labs for now, next in 4 weeks unless worse. Small frequent meals with enzymes.
2. Severe AUD: frank talk with both of them; this is the third serious alcohol complication. He says he's done. Program info again; brother will drive him to an intake if he calls.
3. Weight 54.

documents.title: Liver tests
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Rohan, good progress: bilirubin is down to 1.8, clotting test 1.2 and platelets 128, all moving the right way. Keep doing what you're doing. See you in August.

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT / OBSERVATION RECORD
Arrival 11/02/2025 11:10. Discharged from observation 11/04/2025.

Brought in by family for confusion and agitation. Severe alcohol use disorder, history of alcoholic hepatitis earlier this year. Was drinking heavily until two days ago and has had nothing since.

BP 160/100, HR 120, RR 22, T 38.2 C.
Tremulous, sweaty, anxious. Oriented to self only, not to place or date. Nonfocal neurologic exam.

Na 140, K 4.0, Cl 100, BUN 18, Cr 1.0. AST 72, ALT 50, GGT 300. MCV 96.
ECG: sinus tachycardia, no other abnormality.

Assessment: alcohol withdrawal, uncomplicated (no seizures, no hallucinations).
Treatment: symptom-triggered lorazepam, IV thiamine, fluids; placed in observation. Mental status cleared by the following morning; CIWA scores low by day 2.

Discharged home with family. Home medications unchanged. Primary care follow-up within the week; outpatient addiction treatment resources provided.

documents.title: Call from brother
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Brother: took Rohan to the ED yesterday, confused and shaking after he stopped drinking Friday. Kept overnight, more himself this morning. Booked follow-up 11/13. Records requested.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ED/observation record 11/2-11/4 reviewed: withdrawal with confusion, cleared overnight on lorazepam, no seizures.

He remembers little of the first day. Drinking had crept back up over September and October to every night, then he stopped on his own that Friday. Has not had a drink since the ED. Shaky for a couple of days, now fine.
BP normal today, HR 80s. No tremor. Oriented, conversational.

A/P: alcohol withdrawal episode, resolved. Severe AUD with a growing list of complications. Long conversation: next time he stops he needs medical help to do it; never alone. He and his brother have the ED plan. Offered referral to an addiction medicine clinic: he'll "think on it." Labs today. Thiamine daily. RTC 6 to 8 weeks.

documents.title: ICU Discharge Summary
documents.author: critical care
documents.body:
BRIEF DISCHARGE SUMMARY (ICU / MEDICINE)
Admitted 01/11/2026 via the ED, discharged 01/17/2026.

Diagnosis: delirium tremens.
Background: severe alcohol use disorder; chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency; alcoholic cerebellar degeneration; alcoholic liver disease. ED visit for withdrawal with confusion about two months earlier.

Presentation: about 12 hours of mounting anxiety, hand tremor and heavy sweating after stopping alcohol abruptly; last drink roughly 36 hours before arrival. He had been drinking about a pint of vodka a day in the preceding months.
BP 160/100, HR 120, RR 22, T 37.8 C. Agitated, diaphoretic, tremulous, disoriented to time and place. No focal neurologic deficit.

Labs on arrival: Na 140, K 4.0, Cl 100, BUN 18, Cr 1.1, glucose 90, Mg 1.8, Ca 9.2, AST 72, ALT 50, alkaline phosphatase 90. CBC including platelets within normal limits.

Course: admitted to the ICU. Escalating benzodiazepines with adjunctive phenobarbital, high-dose IV thiamine, electrolyte repletion. Did not require intubation. Delirium cleared by day 4; transferred to the floor and discharged home on day 7.

Discharge medications: home medications unchanged. Follow-up with primary care.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, high MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here for a routine follow-up and tells me he was in the ICU earlier this month. We heard nothing from the hospital.

His account, with his brother filling in: had switched from beer to vodka over the fall, about a pint a day. Decided to quit cold on his own around the 9th. Within a day and a half he was shaking, sweating, frightened; brother called 911. Spent most of a week in the hospital, several days in the ICU, "out of my head" for the first few. Told it was DTs. No seizure that he knows of. No new medicines at discharge.

Today: calm, oriented, no tremor. HR 84. Weight 54.
PHQ-9 7; low mood since, no SI.

A/P
1. Delirium tremens, 1/2026, by patient and family report; records requested. Added to problem list.
2. Severe AUD: two withdrawal hospitalizations in ten weeks, now DTs. Told him directly that the next unsupervised stop could kill him. If he wants to quit again (he says he does), it has to be through a medically supervised detox; gave the program number and said I would call with him. He said not today. Brother on board.
3. Labs today.
RTC 4 weeks.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Doing OK. Says he is drinking "just beer, just weekends" since February. Brother not here today. Mood better (PHQ-9 4). Working again, ground level. Stools fine; taking enzymes. Gait unchanged, no new falls.
O: Calm, no tremor. Anicteric. Abdomen soft. Wide-based gait.
A/P: DTs episode in January, resolved; history kept in the narrative. AUD: less than before by report. Reiterated: if he stops, he calls us first. Still declines a program. LFTs, GGT, CBC. Thiamine/folate/MVI refilled. RTC 3 months.

No intracranial hemorrhage. No mass effect or midline shift. No acute territorial infarct. Ventricles and basal cisterns patent. Calvarium intact.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 07/14/2026, discharged 07/20/2026.

Diagnoses: community-acquired pneumonia; alcohol withdrawal seizures.
Background: severe alcohol use disorder with prior withdrawal including delirium tremens (01/2026); chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency; alcoholic cerebellar degeneration; alcoholic liver disease. NKDA.

Course: admitted with pneumonia on chest x-ray and started on IV ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin. Last alcohol about 24 hours before admission. On hospital day 2 (7/15) he grew agitated and tremulous and said he felt jittery. He denied headache, chest pain or breathlessness. T 37.8 C, BP 160/100, HR 110, RR 18. Diaphoretic, coarse tremor of the outstretched hands, anxious. Electrolytes, renal function and liver enzymes normal; blood alcohol undetectable. Later that day he had two brief generalized seizures, treated with IV lorazepam; symptom-triggered benzodiazepines thereafter. CT head showed no acute abnormality. No further seizures. Antiseizure medication not indicated for withdrawal seizures. Antibiotics completed (5 days) before discharge; afebrile, eating, ambulating at baseline.

Discharge medications: home medications unchanged (pancrelipase, thiamine, folic acid, multivitamin).

Follow-up: primary care in 1 to 2 weeks. Repeat chest x-ray in 6 to 8 weeks to document resolution. Strongly advised abstinence through a supervised program.

documents.title: Call from brother
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Brother called: Rohan admitted Tuesday with pneumonia, then had seizures yesterday from withdrawal. Stable today per brother. Will book post-discharge visit once he knows the date. Records requested.

procedures.procedure: Transitional care management, high complexity

documents.title: Post-hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Discharge summary (7/14-7/20) reviewed: pneumonia, then two withdrawal seizures on day 2. CT head negative.

He feels tired but better. Cough mostly gone, no fever, breathing fine. No further seizures; doesn't remember them. Has not had a drink since admission, about two weeks; brother confirms. Not driving.

Exam: afebrile, RR and SpO2 normal. Lungs with good air movement, clear today. Heart regular. Calm, no tremor. Wide-based gait at baseline.

A/P
1. CAP: clinically resolving. Repeat 2-view CXR in early to mid September per the hospital; ordered.
2. Alcohol withdrawal seizures: single episode in hospital, no recurrence. No driving per state rules for now; discussed.
3. Severe AUD: withdrawal seizures now on top of DTs in January. Very direct conversation. He says he's "really done" this time. Gave the supervised program number again and offered to call together; he asked for a week to think.
4. Labs today.
RTC mid-September after the x-ray.
